claims.text: Elevated-temperature degradation of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 is primarily governed by selective surface oxidation of Cr and Al.
The additive-manufacturing-derived fine, nonequilibrium microstructure accelerates selective oxidation.
Cr and Al oxidation initially produces a protective oxide scale.
The oxide scale is thin and ultimately unstable under thermal cycling.
Thermal cycling causes oxide-scale spallation and initiates localized degradation.
Localized surface degradation occurs without compromising the overall mechanical integrity of the underlying fcc matrix.
The as-built Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has a single-phase fcc matrix.
Rapid additive solidification gives this alloy a refined microstructure with a high grain-boundary density.
The additively manufactured alloy may contain microsegregation or local compositional variations.
Elevated-temperature exposure forms and evolves Cr/Al-rich surface oxide scales, potentially with secondary Ti oxides.
Oxidation also proceeds along additive-manufacturing-derived fast diffusion paths such as grain boundaries.
At elevated temperature, Cr and Al diffuse to the surface and oxidize preferentially.
High grain-boundary density and local compositional variations cause heterogeneous oxide growth and stress accumulation.
Heterogeneous oxide growth and accumulated stress cause eventual oxide-scale spallation.
Under oxidizing conditions, spallation exposes fresh metal and promotes further oxidation.
Under reducing conditions, low oxygen partial pressure hinders coherent oxide formation and produces internally driven degradation.
Oxidizing exposure will produce a heterogeneous Cr/Al-rich scale that eventually spalls.
Reducing exposure will produce a thinner or less adherent oxide scale than oxidizing exposure.
Both oxidizing and reducing exposures will measurably alter oxide composition and microstructure relative to the as-built state.
Porosity and residual stresses introduced by variations in additive manufacturing may alter diffusion pathways and degradation kinetics.
